title: Database Transactions & Isolation: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on transaction control, savepoints, isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent, row locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE, and deadlocks.

chapters.title: Transactions: The Mental Model
points: A transaction is a group of statements that succeed or fail as one unit; ACID = Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (constraints hold before and after), Isolated (concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work), Durable (committed data survives a crash)
Mental model: changes made inside a transaction are private until COMMIT; ROLLBACK throws them all away
Autocommit: by default each standalone statement is its own transaction; BEGIN switches to manual control until COMMIT/ROLLBACK
Durability comes from the write-ahead log (WAL): the log is flushed to disk at COMMIT, data pages are written later
Atomicity is implemented by undo/rollback info (MVCC old row versions in Postgres, undo log in MySQL InnoDB)

chapters.title: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and Savepoints
points: Core workflow: BEGIN (or START TRANSACTION); run statements; COMMIT to persist or ROLLBACK to undo everything
Example: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT;
SAVEPOINT sp1 marks a point inside the transaction; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1 undoes only work after it and keeps the transaction open; RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp1 discards the marker

In Postgres an error aborts the whole transaction (state 'current transaction is aborted'); every later statement fails until ROLLBACK or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint, which is how you recover from one failed statement
MySQL DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP) causes an implicit commit; Postgres DDL is transactional and can be rolled back

chapters.title: Isolation Levels and Read Anomalies
points: Dirty read: reading another transaction's uncommitted change, which may later be rolled back
Non-repeatable read: the same row read twice in one transaction returns different values because another transaction committed an UPDATE/DELETE in between
Phantom read: re-running the same range query returns a different set of rows because another transaction committed an INSERT/DELETE matching the predicate
Four levels: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads; READ COMMITTED prevents dirty only; REPEATABLE READ also prevents non-repeatable reads; SERIALIZABLE prevents all three

Defaults and quirks: Postgres and Oracle default to READ COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB to REPEATABLE READ; Postgres treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED; Postgres REPEATABLE READ (snapshot isolation) also blocks phantoms but allows write skew; set with SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE right after BEGIN

chapters.title: SELECT FOR UPDATE and Row Locking
points: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the returned rows until COMMIT/ROLLBACK; other writers and other FOR UPDATE readers on those rows block, plain SELECTs do not under MVCC
Use it for read-modify-write: BEGIN; SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; compute in app; UPDATE ...; COMMIT; this prevents the lost update
FOR SHARE (Postgres) / LOCK IN SHARE MODE (MySQL) allows other readers but blocks writers
NOWAIT errors immediately if a row is locked; SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows, which is the standard pattern for job queues
Locks only the rows matched, so an unindexed WHERE can lock many rows (InnoDB locks every row it scans); always lock by indexed key

chapters.title: Deadlocks and Common Mistakes
points: Deadlock: transaction A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1; neither can proceed
The database detects the cycle and aborts one victim with an error (Postgres 40P01, MySQL error 1213); the victim must ROLLBACK and be retried
Prevention: acquire locks in a consistent order (e.g. always update the lower account id first), keep transactions short, and lock all needed rows up front with one SELECT ... FOR UPDATE ORDER BY id
Mistake: holding a transaction open during user input or an external API call keeps locks and blocks vacuum/cleanup; do slow work outside the transaction
Mistake: no retry logic; SERIALIZABLE failures (Postgres 40001 serialization_failure) and deadlocks are expected and the app must retry the whole transaction

chapters.title: Transactions Cheat Sheet
points: Control: BEGIN; ... COMMIT; | ROLLBACK; | SAVEPOINT s; | ROLLBACK TO s; | RELEASE s;

Anomaly vs level matrix: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty/non-repeatable/phantom; READ COMMITTED allows non-repeatable/phantom; REPEATABLE READ allows phantom (standard SQL; not in Postgres or InnoDB with MVCC); SERIALIZABLE allows none
Set level: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; (Postgres) or SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL ... (before first statement)
Locking: FOR UPDATE (exclusive), FOR SHARE (shared), NOWAIT (fail fast), SKIP LOCKED (queues)
Rules of thumb: keep transactions short, lock in a fixed order, retry on 40P01/40001/1213, default to READ COMMITTED and raise the level only for a proven anomaly
